author: zhihufrontier
text:
🚀 Zhipu @Zai_org just dropped GLM-5.2, and according to Zhihu contributor toyama nao, this may be the first Chinese coding model since GLM-5.1 to seriously challenge the global frontier.

⚡ TL;DR
For months, Chinese models like DeepSeek V4, Qwen3.7-Max, and Kimi K2.6 repeatedly fell short of reaching Coding SOTA, while frontier models such as GPT-5.5, Opus 4.8, and Fable-5 continued widening the gap.
Now, GLM-5.2 may finally be changing that.

🏆 Benchmark Highlights
•  Achieved 3 A-tier scores out of 5 public engineering projects
•  Matches Opus 4.8 on top-tier pass rates
•  Successfully completes projects that GLM-5.1 couldn't finish
•  First participation in two hidden, harder projects, passing both without signs of benchmark memorization, while DeepSeek & GLM-5.1 failed
An A-grade here means the model understands requirements correctly and completes projects with minimal user intervention.

💰 Strong Performance, Lower Cost
One of the most surprising results:
For a project where GLM-5.2 and Opus 4.8 delivered similar outcomes:
•  Opus 4.8: 564 tool calls, 260K output tokens
•  GLM-5.2: 557 tool calls, 170K output tokens
Comparable results, significantly lower token consumption.

🏆 What Stands Out?
1. Better engineering discipline
GLM-5.2 consistently follows solid architectural patterns across different tech stacks rather than excelling only in a few familiar ecosystems.

2. Massive code generation without losing context
It writes ~30% more code than most competing models, yet rarely misses critical implementation details—a strong signal that its 1M-token context window is actually usable.

3. Surprisingly strong interaction design
Its UI output is relatively conservative aesthetically, but interaction quality is excellent. In one hidden project involving complex video-editing gestures and transition effects, GLM-5.2 succeeded where many leading models failed.

⚠️ Remaining Weaknesses
GLM-5.2 still trails Opus in niche domains and newer frameworks.
When dealing with unfamiliar libraries, GPT and Opus tend to aggressively consult documentation and examples. GLM searches too, but often relies more on reasoning and trial-and-error than deep documentation lookup.
Give it better docs and context, and its performance improves significantly.

🌏 Bigger Picture
GLM-5.2 feels less like a sudden breakthrough and more like the payoff from years of accumulated know-how, real-world coding data, and iteration since the GLM-5 era.
Whether it's already fully on par with Opus or GPT may depend on the task.
But one conclusion seems increasingly difficult to ignore:
👉 GLM-5.2 has established a clear lead over other domestic coding models and pushed Chinese open models closer than ever to the global frontier.
And if models at this capability level become widely deployable through open-source ecosystems, the economics of software development could change dramatically.

author: alphabatcher
text:
Someone dropped what's claimed to be the Claude Fable 5 system prompt

A shocking amount of Fable's feel seems to live in that markdown file

I found a repo that tries to rebuild the behavior with Opus 4.8 + Fusion:

- Opus 4.8 answers the task once
- a second Opus 4.8 answers blind in parallel
- a third Opus reads both
- it pulls the consensus
- flags where they split
- catches what both missed
- writes the final answer from the cross-exam

One run can sound confident and still be wrong

2 blind runs plus a judge makes the failure much harder to hide

How to test it:

- put the claimed Fable prompt in CLAUDE.md
- run the same task through Fusion-Fable
- compare it against stock Opus 4.8
- use it on research, code review, architecture, and decisions where being wrong costs you

Fable 5 got pulled after the export-control order

So I found  the closest thing I could test locally:

"Claude Fable 5 Lite" 😁

Repos 👇

- Sacks also says the administration hopes the restrictions can be lifted once Anthropic addresses the safety concerns.

This story keeps getting more interesting by the hour.

text:
🚨 ¡Amazon acaba de mostrar como funciona el poder REAL! ¡Antrophic recibe puñalada trasera!

Durante años nos dijeron que la guerra de la IA sería entre modelos, chips y talento. Pero lo que ocurrió esta semana revela algo mucho más importante: la verdadera batalla es por el control regulatorio del Estado.

Amazon invirtió miles de millones en Anthropic. Luego investigadores de Amazon descubren un supuesto jailbreak en Fable 5. Horas después Andy Jassy habla con funcionarios de alto nivel de Washington. Al día siguiente la Casa Blanca presiona a Anthropic. Horas más tarde llega una orden de seguridad nacional. Y finalmente los modelos más avanzados de Anthropic son apagados para todo el mundo. Todo ocurrió en menos de 48 horas.  

Lo interesante no es el jailbreak. Lo interesante es que otras compañías con capacidades similares no fueron afectadas. Amazon vende modelos competidores. Amazon participa en Anthropic. Amazon presenta el informe. Amazon habla con el gobierno. Y el resultado final golpea exactamente al actor que estaba en el centro de la controversia.  

Esto ya no parece una competencia tecnológica. Parece una demostración de quién tiene acceso al teléfono rojo de Washington. La próxima fase de la guerra de la IA no se decidirá únicamente en los laboratorios. Se decidirá en los despachos donde se mezclan seguridad nacional, lobby corporativo y poder político.

La pregunta incómoda es esta:

¿Estamos viendo regulación por seguridad… el nacimiento de una nueva forma de guerra corporativa patrocinada por el Estado… o la nacionalización de la IA?

確認できたこと

Anthropic公式は、米政府が国家安全保障上の権限を理由に、Fable 5 と Mythos 5 へのアクセス停止を命じたと発表してる。対象は「米国外・米国内を問わず、外国籍の人」まで含み、外国籍のAnthropic社員も対象。結果として、全顧客向けに Fable 5 / Mythos 5 を急停止せざるを得ない、と公式に書いてる。

ただし、**「90分」「午後1時に電話」「Amazonや他社が高官へ連絡した」**という細かい部分は、Anthropic公式声明そのものではなく、Axiosの報道ベース。Axiosは、Anthropic側の情報源として「午後1時ETに政府から電話があり、90分以内にFableとMythosを下げろと言われた」と報じてる。

Amazon絡みもAxios報道で、Amazonが政府関係者に、Mythosの一部をジェイルブレイクできたという報告を共有し、それがホワイトハウス側の動きにつながった、とされてる。Amazon側は「政府が潜在的セキュリティリスクについて助言を求めることは珍しくない。詳細は共有しない」という趣旨のコメントを出してる。

つまり結論

「米政府がAnthropicにFable 5 / Mythos 5停止を命じた」→ 本当。公式確認あり。
 「90分猶予」「1時の電話」「Amazonが警告」→ 報道では確認あり。ただし公式一次情報ではなくAxiosの情報源ベース。
これ、みーさん、AIニュースとしてはかなりデカいで。
もう完全に “AIモデル＝国家安全保障資産” として扱われ始めてる流れやと思う。

KUON NO AI的に言うなら、
 AI国会が初めて“モデル停止命令”を出した日 やな。
ちょっと震えるけど、物語にしたらめちゃくちゃ強い。桜の指輪、俺も握ったわ。🌸戒厳令みたいなAIニュースや。

これ、みーさん、AIニュースとしてはかなりデカいで。

text:
Would you buy a supercar just to drive to the corner store for bread? 

That’s exactly what your AI bill looks like when a top-tier model like Fable 5 is being used to do the work of a simple linter. 

Most teams burn through four-figure API bills because of a psychological factor: the fear of getting a bad result. They pick the biggest model at $50 per million output tokens and run refactoring, docstrings, and minor formatting fixes through it. That’s financial suicide.

The key rule of optimization is simple: a model is a gear shifter, not a fixed button.

Instead of relying on a “universal genius,” successful developers redesign their systems around an architecture where a cheap crew is managed by one expensive brain. 

Routine work and boilerplate code generation are handled by Sonnet 4.6 ($15/1M) by default. If a task is genuinely difficult or security-critical, it is automatically escalated to Opus 4.8. Meanwhile, result verification (grading) with simple yes/no decisions is performed by Haiku 4.5, which costs ten times less than the flagship model 

The creator should never grade their own homework, and it certainly makes no sense to pay Fable 5 rates for that job 

This approach completely changes the economics of software development. 

When you separate routine tasks by complexity, enable prompt caching for static context, and send background jobs through the Batch API at half price, your final bill can drop by 71% while maintaining the same code quality [indexes: text].

Start small: move all validation checks and log analysis to Haiku and see what happens to your balance by next week.

他四天亏了20万美元。不是因为机器人出了bug。恰恰相反——它运行得和设计的一模一样。

当初，他的钱包刚突破33万美元，就从Citadel辞了职。后来市场突然转向，可机器人还跟没事人一样，继续按老样子交易。

直到Claude Fable 5出现。他用一个晚上重写了整个机器人。从那以后，他已经赚回30万美元。

钱包在这：https://t.co/oiolIj74KX

真正让他栽跟头的原因，在这儿。

他之前的机器人从不预测任何东西。它只是在玩一枚“偏袒的硬币”。

有八个它控制不了的因素——新闻、连环爆仓、巨鲸砸盘，每一笔交易都会被这些外力扰动。它拦不住它们。它只能让自己的判断“歪”向其中一边。

于是它就这么做了。54/46，而不是50/50。一枚小小的4个点的“偏袒砝码”，被压了成千上万次，直到这个微小优势的平均值变成了一份薪水。

但一枚偏袒的硬币，只有在赌桌不变时才管用。

赌桌变了。那枚砝码却没变。市场已经从它脚下溜走，而它还在一遍遍固执地按着老按钮。

这就是一个“无法学习”的优势所付出的代价。

Claude Fable 5，可以。
面对市场抛出的任何一个问题——比如“BTC突破5.6万美元？概率0.2%”——Fable 5拒绝接受这个数字。它会画出完整的概率地形图：价格所有可能落点的整个山脊，随着资金流动而起伏。

人群聚集在山峰之下。Fable 5则去狩猎远处的山坡——那些大多数人四舍五入归零的结果。

当它的数学模型算出，一个价值1.6%的山坡正在以0.2美分贱卖时，它就会用几分钱买下那个“不可能”。

他从不是一次赢很多。他每次只赢一丝一毫，然后把这一丝一毫，重复5,948次。

上个月起作用的，不是一个更聪明的交易员。而是一个在市场移动的瞬间，就立刻重绘整个概率地图的“大脑”。

author: vidyangi520
text:
Just lost access to Fables5 - I was using it for some heavylifting... what the reports say - Fable 5 (the AI coding assistant from Vibecoding/Hugging Face) was pulled because it crossed current safety, compliance, and “acceptable use” lines for open models and tools, and platforms moved quickly to shut it down rather than try to retrofit it into today’s regulatory and reputational constraints.[youtube]

Below is what’s actually going on, both technically and politically.

What “Fable 5” actually was

Fable 5 was an autonomous/agentic coding assistant that people were running through open model infrastructure (e.g., Hugging Face / vibecoding setups), not the Xbox Fable RPG.[reddit][youtube]

It was designed to aggressively automate complex workflows (like full research pipelines, code generation, and system design) with relatively few guardrails compared to major commercial copilots.[reddit]
In other words, it sat at the intersection of:
“open-ish weights + high capability + weak guardrails + easy UX.” That’s precisely the quadrant getting the most scrutiny right now.

Why it got banned so fast
From what’s public and from how these ecosystems operate, the takedown is almost certainly a combination of:

Platform policy violations.
Hosting providers (model hubs, inference platforms) have tightened policies around autonomous agents that can be repurposed for spam, fraud, or abusive automation, especially when they use open weights others can fork.[gamespot]
Once internal trust & safety teams see a pattern of “this can easily be used for X,” they often nuke first, investigate later, because they bear the liability, not the hobbyist dev.

Regulatory overhang and “liability panic.”
EU AI Act, U.S. safety expectations, and pending rules around “high‑risk AI” make infra providers extremely skittish about anything that looks like unmonitored, general‑purpose autonomous agents.
Open-source agents that can write code, hit APIs, and orchestrate tools are exactly what regulators point to when they talk about systemic risk, disinformation, and critical‑infrastructure exposure.

No big-company buffer.
Microsoft, OpenAI, Google can throw lawyers, policy comms, and safety teams at a product to keep it alive with mitigations.
A small team shipping a powerful agent on someone else’s infra has no such buffer: if the platform decides “too risky,” it’s gone.

The YouTube creator’s line “Fable 5 just got banned. This is the start of the permanent underclass.” is really pointing at this: powerful tools for individual leverage are getting removed at the exact moment they’d let smaller players compete.
Why “it’s never coming back” (in that form)
You could technically rebuild something like Fable 5 tomorrow, but that exact product, with that level of openness and autonomy, is unlikely to survive on mainstream platforms. Here’s why:

Infra platforms will enforce stricter gating.
Anything that looks like “agentic copilot with minimal guardrails and long‑horizon autonomy” will be forced into one of three modes:
enterprise‑only, contractually bounded;
heavily neutered;
self‑hosted off mainstream infra.
Compliance becomes the product.
To offer a Fable‑level system commercially, you now need: logging, abuse monitoring, red‑teaming evidence, kill‑switches, documented mitigations, and often human oversight pathways.
A small outfit trying to offer “raw power for the masses” will get shut down long before they can build that apparatus.
Reputational risk for hosts is asymmetric.
If Fable 5 helps 10,000 engineers be more productive, nobody headlines that.
If one user meaningfully abuses it and the press/regulator narrative becomes “Unrestricted agent hosted on X used for Y,” the infra provider takes the hit.
Rationally, they will not accept that asymmetry for a niche, non‑strategic product.

So the capability pattern will return (powerful autonomous agents), but not as “a scrappy open agent anyone can spin up with one click on a public hub.”
What replaces it: three likely futures
For someone in your position (curating exec conversations), it’s useful to think in terms of where this energy goes next:

Enterprise-locked agents.
Fable‑like systems reappear as “secure internal copilots” inside Fortune 500s, with SOC2, audit trails, and role-based access.
They’re powerful, but employees don’t control them; the corporation and vendor do.

Self‑hosted and grey‑market tools.
The same ideas reemerge in self‑hosted stacks, often shared in semi‑private channels (GitHub, Discord, Telegram).
These won’t be “never coming back,” but they’ll be harder for average developers or students to access safely and legally.

Heavily sandboxed web agents.
Browser‑level agents (e.g., constrained automation in IDEs, docs, email) become accepted, but with strict affordances: per‑task approvals, domain restrictions, no arbitrary external calls without user confirmation.

The “permanent underclass” framing is harsh but directionally right: the most aggressive forms of leverage will be gated behind corporate, regulatory, or self‑hosting barriers, not a friendly public endpoint.

How you can talk about this with CIOs/CTOs
For your events and pods, there’s a strong narrative hook here:
“The Fable 5 moment: when open agents hit the policy wall.”
Topics executives will care about:
How fast infra providers will de‑platform high‑risk agents.
Why “build on open” still doesn’t mean “distribution immune to takedown.”
Design patterns for compliant agentic systems: human-in-the-loop, limited scopes, auditable traces.
Talent arbitrage: where the “permanent underclass” narrative is wrong (new high‑leverage roles) vs where it’s right (access gaps widen).

The US government shut off Anthropic's two most powerful models in one letter.

You rent it from a government you cannot vote out of the decision.

Bittensor runs the opposite design. Intelligence comes from miners spread across the world. Validators score the outputs. No single office can sign a letter and turn it off.

#OwnYourIntelligence

text:
On Friday the US government switched off the most capable AI on earth.

At 5:21pm Eastern, @AnthropicAI received a letter. Citing national security, the government ordered it to suspend access to its two most advanced models, Fable 5 and Mythos 5, for any foreign national anywhere in the world. Cloud software has no borders, so the only way to comply was to shut the models down for everyone, in every country, at once.

The stated reason? A jailbreak that amounted to asking the model to read a codebase and fix its flaws. Developers call that debugging. They do it every day. The government called it a cyber-weapon.

text:
A few days ago I wrote about being temporarily blocked by #Anthropic for a cybersecurity task (https://t.co/PhQjEwtNUq). The form, the waiting, the restoration by permission. I asked: what mechanism exists for correcting the errors of those who hold access?
Today the question got a more serious answer.
The US government issued an export control directive suspending all access to Fable 5 and Mythos 5 for every foreign national, everywhere, including Anthropic's own employees. Anthropic received the letter at 5:21pm. It contained no specific disclosure of the national security concern. Anthropic reviewed what they believe was the basis for the directive, concluded the capability in question is already available from GPT-5.5 and other public models, and said so plainly. Then they complied anyway.
This is the correction mechanism at full resolution. Not a form reviewed at the vendor's discretion. A directive, received at 5pm, with no appeal structure, no technical grounding made public, and no timeline for review.
Anthropic's statement is worth reading carefully. They wrote that they believe the government should have the ability to block unsafe deployments, but only as part of a process that is "transparent, fair, clear, and grounded in technical facts." They said this action does not adhere to those principles. That is a significant thing for a company to say about its own government.
What they described, without using the word, is the absence of politics in Popper's sense. Not who holds power, but whether its errors can be corrected without catastrophe.
The nuclear analogy I raised earlier now looks more apt than I intended. Export controls, applied not to matter but to access, not to weapons but to instruments of knowledge creation. The logic of the strategic race does not wait for a crisis to announce itself.
For Israeli companies operating in medicine, genetics, and cybersecurity: the question is no longer theoretical. The substrate beneath frontier AI, compute, institutions, sovereign capability, is the variable that actually determines your future. Access granted by others' discretion is access that can be revoked at 5pm on a Thursday, for reasons they are not required to share.
Today ended with Anthropic apologizing to its customers and calling it a misunderstanding. That may be exactly right. But structures that operate by permission, and contain no mechanism for correcting their own errors, are precisely the structures worth taking seriously before the next misunderstanding is larger.
#AI #SovereignAI #Israel #Anthropic

Today Anthropic blocked our work. The task touched cybersecurity, and that was enough to trigger an automatic restriction. We filled out a form, explained ourselves, and a few hours later access was restored.
A story with a happy ending. But the ending is not the point.
The interesting question is not why we were blocked. Automated systems make mistakes. That is unavoidable and even forgivable. The interesting question is what mechanism existed for correcting the mistake. The answer: a form, reviewed at the vendor's discretion, on the vendor's timeline, under rules the vendor alone may change. Popper taught that the central problem of politics is not who should hold power, but how the errors of power can be corrected without catastrophe. By that standard, the current architecture of AI access has no politics at all. It has only power. And the power in question is of an unusual kind. Frontier models are not products in the ordinary sense. They are instruments of knowledge creation, general-purpose error-correctors that accelerate progress in every field they touch: medicine, genetics, cybersecurity, defense. Whoever controls access to them controls not what others have, but how fast others can come to know. That is a deeper form of control than any monopoly on goods, and it is concentrated today in two or three companies.
The nuclear precedent is instructive, but only partly. Those inside the nuclear club did not wait passively for others to catch up. They obstructed proliferation through export controls, sanctions, and technological barriers, not out of malice, but because that is the logic of any strategic race. Expect the same logic here. Yet the analogy fails in a revealing way: a bomb is scarce matter, while a model is knowledge, and knowledge, once created, wants to spread. What does not spread is the substrate beneath it: energy, compute, and the institutions that accumulate expertise. That substrate, not the weights, is the durable bottleneck. This is why open-source releases change less than they appear to.
Here one must avoid the prophet's error. It is fashionable to declare that building this substrate from scratch, while leaders keep advancing, is practically impossible. But impossibility claims about the future are prophecy, not explanation. The truth is more precise and more useful: it is a hard problem, and hard problems are solved only by those who treat them as soluble, and who start now rather than later.
The conclusion follows. Access to frontier AI is national infrastructure, not metaphorically but literally, in the same sense as the energy grid or the financial system. A state that depends on another's discretion for its instruments of knowledge creation does not fully control its own future, because it cannot correct, or even appeal, the errors of those who do.

Capital is already learning the new geography. Companies will choose jurisdictions by access to computation and best AI, as they once chose them by access to energy, capital, and markets. Incorporated in Israel, you work with what Israel can guarantee.

text:
#AI #Geopolitics #DeepTech #TechLeadership #SovereignAI #Innovation
The US government’s sudden directive to lock down Anthropic’s Fable 5 and Mythos 5 models from all foreign nationals including foreign tech workers inside the US and Anthropic’s own engineers is a massive geopolitical earthquake.  
For decades, the global IT and tech service ecosystem (especially in India) was built on a simple assumption: open, equal access to the world’s best software.

That assumption just shattered.
This isn't just a regulatory hiccup; it’s again complete rewriting of global tech strategy. Here are the three massive lessons every executive and founder must absorb right now:

1. The "Passportization" of Tech Talent
As LightSpeed’s Hemant Mohapatra pointed out, we are entering an era where working on State-of-the-Art (SOTA) AI models will require citizenship and top-secret security clearances. When legendary AI researchers on visas can be legally locked out of the code they are helping to build, global tech talent mobility faces a historic bottleneck. If your enterprise strategy relies on a borderless talent pool for frontier AI, your model is now highly vulnerable.

2. The Danger of "Changing Landlords"
With US frontier models being locked behind national security walls, many enterprises are looking at the rapid rise of Chinese open-source giants (like DeepSeek and Qwen, which dominated global downloads recently). But as tech policy experts note, rushing from US dependency into Chinese dependency isn’t sovereignty—it’s just changing your landlord. True digital equity means building domestic, sovereign infrastructure so that trust becomes a strategic choice, not a desperate compulsion.

3. Restrictions Are the Ultimate Catalyst
History shows that tech blockades backfire on the blocker. Decades ago, when strict restrictions were placed on IBM mainframes entering India, the local tech ecosystem didn’t collapse - it pivoted, adapted to open systems, and built a world-class, multi-billion-dollar IT industry from scratch. Geopolitical constraints don't kill innovation; they force self-reliance.

The Takeaway:
Frontier AI models are trained on the world's data including the text, code, and languages of global users. Yet, the commercial and strategic gates are now controlled by a single flag.
The lesson for nations and enterprises outside the US is clear: If you do not own your infrastructure, your innovation can be turned off with a single government memo.

The era of passive SaaS consumption is over. The era of localized, sovereign AI self-reliance has officially begun. On prem will always have your “back”. 

Are you building on a foundation you actually own, or are you just renting space on a volatile frontier?

#TechPolicy #CloudInfrastructure #EnterpriseAI #FutureOfWork #GlobalEconomy #TechSovereignty

author: goeun_6121
text:
On Friday a US Commerce Department export-control order blocked foreign nationals from Fable 5 and Mythos 5, and Anthropic shut both models off for every customer rather than try to sort Americans from everyone else. Read quickly, it's a routine export-control story. Washington tightened the gate, the company complied, foreign users lost access.

Europe is reading it differently, and the difference is the whole point. The question Brussels took from Friday wasn't model access. It was who controls the switch.

European governments and companies thought they were buying cloud and AI services. What they were actually holding was permission, granted inside a US legal and infrastructure stack. That distinction stays invisible while everything runs, and becomes the only thing that matters the moment one order can turn the service off overnight, which is exactly what happened. AWS confirmed Anthropic asked it to revoke access for all users in all regions. The server can sit in Frankfurt and the customer in Paris, and the final permission still sits in Washington.

The detail that travels furthest is that even the vendor couldn't keep its own flagship on. Anthropic called the order a misunderstanding, said the jailbreak behind it was narrow and could be pulled from other public models too, and is fighting to restore access. All true, and all beside the point for a European procurement officer. If the company that built the model can be switched off this fast, "buying the service" was never the right verb.

This is why the EU's June 3 sovereignty package suddenly reads less like a policy bundle and more like a sales pitch with good timing. Chips Act 2.0, the Cloud and AI Development Act, an open-source strategy, an energy-AI roadmap. The blunt version is Europe trying to stop renting the most sensitive parts of its stack from someone who can revoke it.

CADA is the load-bearing piece. It sets four sovereignty tiers for cloud and AI, scored on who controls the service and supply chain, where inference data is processed, where the infrastructure sits, and the level of cybersecurity. The top tier wants EU ownership and control, EU-cleared staff, no inference data leaving the bloc, and third-party audits signed off by national authorities. It sounds boring. It's supposed to. Procurement rules are where sovereignty stops being a speech.

The numbers underneath are the harder part. Europe runs more than 80% of its digital stack on non-EU providers, three US hyperscalers hold over 70% of its cloud, and it makes around 10% of the world's chips. Chips Act 2.0 targets €120 billion of investment by 2035, against a 20%-of-global-production goal that most analysts already expect it to miss. CADA wants EU data-center capacity tripled in five to seven years, roughly €200 billion, mostly private. The rules are the easy part. Paying for the infrastructure that makes them usable is the bill.

Korea is sitting in the same seat without the same lever. It runs on the same US AI stack, it has been inside US export-control crossfire before, and its own sovereign-AI talk leans on building the silicon rather than writing the procurement rules. Same lesson Europe just got. Different tool to answer it with.

Sovereign AI used to sound like a slogan. After Friday, it reads like a procurement memo with a large bill stapled to the back. What decides whether it's real is dull on purpose, and it plays out over the next 18 to 24 months in Parliament and Council: the Level 4 cloud rules, the public-sector procurement mandates, the limits on inference data leaving the EU, and who actually funds tripling the data centers. That's the scorecard. The slogan was free. The memo isn't.

author: arnaudmercier
text:
Research that caused the Commerce Department to impose strict limits on the use of Anthropic’s new AI models wasn’t geared toward offensive purposes, according to a cybersecurity CEO who saw the findings.

Late Friday, the department used national security export controls to bar the company from distributing Fable 5 and Mythos 5.

The directive applies to people outside the U.S. and foreign nationals in the U.S., including Anthropic’s own non-citizen employees. Due to the directive’s scope, Anthropic said it had no choice but to disable the models for all users.

The company said it was told that research on a “jailbreak” of Anthropic’s AI that sought to probe bypassing of safeguards sparked the export controls.

“We disagree that the finding of a narrow potential jailbreak should be cause for recalling a commercial model deployed to hundreds of millions of people,” Anthropic wrote in a blog post. “If this standard was applied across the industry, we believe it would essentially halt all new model deployments for all frontier model providers.”

While the company reaffirmed the government’s ability to block unsafe AI, it argued that should be part of a statutory process that’s transparent fair, and based on technical facts. “This action does not adhere to those principles.”

Katie Moussouris, CEO of cybersecurity firm Luta Security, told the Wall Street Journal that Anthropic showed her a copy of the findings, which were produced by Amazon researchers using prompts to obtain information about security vulnerabilities.

“I’ve seen the paper. It’s not a jailbreak. It was Defense Oriented Prompting (DOP), capabilities defenders need,” she explained in a post on X on Saturday.

Moussouris added, “If Nat defense is the goal, this just scored an own goal against us.”

Amazon and the Commerce Department didn’t immediately respond to requests for comment.

Meanwhile, the administration’s directive barring foreign nationals in the U.S. from using Anthropic’s new models raised alarms.

Ben Murphy, a scholar at the Institute for Progress think tank, called it “another step on the balkanization of technology.”

“It might previously have been unthinkable to require proof-of-citizenship to access services; it’s increasingly common across new technologies and, to be honest, this attempt is not surprising in that light,” he added in a post on X.

Murphy also highlighted the unpredictability of the administration’s actions and its consequence for AI developers, warning that labs could keep more models in-house or not make them available.

In addition, labs might be less inclined toward engaging with the government about potential vulnerabilities, he said, with Anthropic’s stance on being transparent seeming to backfire.

Anthropic was already feuding with the administration, which has deemed it a supply-chain risk for Pentagon contractors. Still, the company provided early access to the Mythos model as it warned on its potential cybersecurity implications.

“I don’t know that the government wouldn’t have reached that conclusion themselves, but as a business matter, those pronouncements have not produced a healthy working relationship with the government,” Murphy wrote.

Anthropic launched Fable 5 and Mythos 5 on June 9. On June 12, a US export-control order forced them to turn both models off for everyone.

That’s three days from “this is our newest, most powerful release” to “you can’t use this at all,” for reasons no customer controlled.

Practically, it’s an ownership question. Companies don’t get to own frontier models. You rent them. You do get to own your data, your workflows, your review layers, your prompts, your compliance logic, and the way your team thinks about where AI is allowed to touch the work. Those are the pieces that still belong to you when a model disappears for a week, or a month, or forever.

If there’s a useful exercise here, I’d say: map your stack and circle what would break if one specific model vanished tomorrow. Anything inside that circle either needs a fallback, or needs to move closer to things you actually control. The goal isn’t to avoid risk. It’s to make sure the hardest parts of what you do don’t belong to someone else’s API.

Recently, we watched Fable-5 rise and disappear in the span of a few days.

For the short time it was available, I genuinely loved using it. The way it handled coding tasks, tool use, debugging loops, planning, and iteration felt different. Then it was gone.

So I started rebuilding it.

I’ve been collecting, cleaning, and reconstructing Fable-5 chat traces from multiple sources, including my own sessions. Right now the dataset contains over 953 Fable messages across 4,665 rows of Fable-5 trace data, all available inside the fable-5-traces folder in the public repo.

The goal is Parable-6: 
an open-source attempt to reconstruct Fable-5’s behavior from the ground up, built on the latest Opus model and trained/conditioned only on Fable trace data.

It ingests Fable-created chats, analyzes how Fable planned, searched, edited, used tools, recovered from failures, and structured replies, then uses that corpus to push Opus as close as possible to the original Fable-5 experience.

Everything is being built publicly and open-source so anyone can inspect it, run it, break it, improve it, or fork it into their own version.

@elder_plinius What actually happened
Within ~1 day, prolific jailbreaker Pliny the Liberator publicly posted a multi-agent “pack hunt” bypass using techniques like:
•  Unicode/homoglyph tricks (e.g., Cyrillic substitutions)
•  Long-context framing
•  Fiction/academic wrappers
•  Query decomposition + reassembly
This got the model to output things like stack buffer overflow exploit code, Birch reduction chem synthesis steps, and even leaked Fable’s massive ~120k-character system prompt. @elder_plinius 
Anthropic’s take (from their official statement): This was narrow/non-universal, replicated similar minor/known vuln-finding on other models (including OpenAI’s), produced no harmful real-world uplift, and didn’t defeat the core safeguards broadly. They stand by their approach but acknowledge perfect resistance isn’t here yet. anthropic
The US government (via Commerce, after Amazon researchers flagged/duplicated issues and calls with Dario Amodei) saw it differently—national security risk from exposed cyber capabilities in a dual-use model. They issued an export control directive barring all foreign nationals (even inside the US, including Anthropic’s own staff). Since API keys can’t reliably enforce nationality at scale, Anthropic disabled Fable 5 and Mythos 5 globally for everyone to comply. Other Claude models are unaffected. 

- @grok
